q-101258.name: Question 1
q-101258.problem:
What is the recursive formula for the following geometric sequence?

$$
20,\,15,\,\frac{45}{4},\,…
$$
q-101258.worked_solution:
The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio $r$ takes the form

$$
{a}_{n+1}=r\cdot {a}_{n}.
$$

In this case, the first term is ${a}_{1}=20,$ and we can calculate the common ratio $r$ as

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{15}{20}=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

Consequently, the recursive formula for this sequence is

$$
{a}_{n+1}=\frac{3}{4}\,{a}_{n},\,{a}_{1}=20,\,n\ge 1.
$$

q-101258.html:
Question 1
?

What is the recursive formula for the following geometric sequence? 20,15,454,…

a
an+1=34an,a1=20,n≥1
b
an+1=320an,a1=15,n≥1
c
an+1=43an,a1=20,n≥1
d
an+1=454an,a1=15,n≥1
e
an+1=38an,a1=20,n≥1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio r takes the form an+1=r⋅an.

In this case, the first term is a1=20, and we can calculate the common ratio r as

r=a2a1=1520=34.

Consequently, the recursive formula for this sequence is

an+1=34an,a1=20,n≥1.

q-249790.name: Question 2
q-249790.problem:
Consider the following geometric sequence:

$$
30,\,50,\,\frac{250}{3},\,…
$$

The recursive formula for this geometric sequence is

${a}_{n+1}=${{field-1}}$,\,{a}_{1}=$
{{field-2}}$,\,n\ge 1.$
q-249790.worked_solution:
The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio $r$ takes the form

$$
{a}_{n+1}=r\cdot {a}_{n}.
$$

In this case, the first term is ${a}_{1}=30,$ and we can calculate the common ratio $r$ as

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{50}{30}=\frac{5}{3}.
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula is

q-109811.name: Question 9
q-109811.problem:
Which of the three sequences below are geometric sequences?

I. $\frac{1}{3},\,-\frac{4}{3},\,-\frac{16}{3},\,…$

II. $-5,\,-20,\,80,\,…$

III. $f(n+1)=4f(n)-4,\,f(1)=2,\,n\ge 1$
q-109811.worked_solution:
A sequence is geometric if there is a common ratio between its terms. Let's check each sequence in turn.

- Sequence I is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{(-\frac{4}{3})}{(\frac{1}{3})}=-4 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-\frac{16}{3})}{(-\frac{4}{3})}=4\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence II is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{-20}{-5}=4 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{80}{-20}=-4\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence III is not a geometric sequence. To see this, we can calculate the first $3$ terms of the sequence and then compute the ratios of consecutive terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1) & =2 \\ f(2) & =4\cdot 2-4=4 \\ f(3) & =4\cdot 4-4=12\end{aligned}
$$

So, the first two pairs of consecutive terms have different ratios:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{f(2)}{f(1)} & =\frac{4}{2}=2 \\ \frac{f(3)}{f(2)} & =\frac{12}{4}=3\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, none of the given is a geometric sequence.

A sequence is geometric if there is a common ratio between its terms. Let's check each sequence in turn.

- Sequence I could be a geometric. For each pair of consecutive terms, the common ratio is the same:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(\frac{1}{2})}{(\frac{3}{2})} & =\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{(\frac{1}{6})}{(\frac{1}{2})} & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence II is not a geometric sequence. To see this, we can calculate the first $3$ terms of the sequence and then compute the ratios of consecutive terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =2 \\ {a}_{2} & =2+{2}^{2}=6 \\ {a}_{3} & =6+{6}^{2}=42\end{aligned}
$$

So, the first two pairs of consecutive terms have different ratios:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{6}{2} & =3 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{42}{6} & =7\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence III is not a geometric sequence. To see this, we can calculate the first $3$ terms of the sequence and then compute the ratios of consecutive terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1) & =\frac{1}{5} \\ f(2) & =5(\frac{1}{5})+3=4 \\ f(3) & =5(4)+3=23\end{aligned}
$$

So, the first two pairs of consecutive terms have different ratios:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{f(2)}{f(1)} & =\frac{4}{(\frac{1}{5})}=20 \\ \frac{f(3)}{f(2)} & =\frac{23}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, only I is a geometric sequence.

Question 10

Which of the three sequences below are geometric sequences?

  1. 32,12,16,…
  2. an+1=an+an2,a1=2,n≥1
  3. f(n+1)=5f(n)+3,f(1)=15,n≥1
a
I and II only
b
I only
c
II only
d
III only
e
None
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A sequence is geometric if there is a common ratio between its terms. Let's check each sequence in turn.

  • Sequence I could be a geometric. For each pair of consecutive terms, the common ratio is the same: (12)(32)=13(16)(12)=13

  • Sequence II is not a geometric sequence. To see this, we can calculate the first 3 terms of the sequence and then compute the ratios of consecutive terms: a1=2a2=2+22=6a3=6+62=42 So, the first two pairs of consecutive terms have different ratios: a2a1=62=3a3a2=426=7

  • Sequence III is not a geometric sequence. To see this, we can calculate the first 3 terms of the sequence and then compute the ratios of consecutive terms: f(1)=15f(2)=5(15)+3=4f(3)=5(4)+3=23 So, the first two pairs of consecutive terms have different ratios: f(2)f(1)=4(15)=20f(3)f(2)=234

In conclusion, only I is a geometric sequence.
